items.title: Aero-VPA: Few-Step Flow-Matching Control over Non-Reconstructive JEPA Latents for Agile Flight on Edge Hardware
items.content: arXiv:2611.04392v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generalize across tasks, but their autoregressive decoders need sequential forward passes in proportion to the action horizon, each bounded below on embedded aerial platforms by streaming billions of parameters from memory. We present Aero-VPA, a lightweight Vision-Predictor-Action architecture for 3D navigation on edge hardware. A compact RGB-D Vision Transformer and a five-head ensemble predictor, trained without pixel reconstruction, forecast the next latent state; a Conditional Flow Matching solver generates a velocity and yaw-rate chunk in two Euler steps, so each decision takes five sequential network evaluations; and the ensemble dispersion drives an uncertainty fallback. Version 1 specified the architecture, deployment and protocol without results. This version reports the first closed-loop evaluation: PX4 software-in-the-loop simulation of quadrotor missions in procedurally generated forests. Behaviour cloning failed on all 60 missions despite open-loop errors of 0.02-0.04 m/s: the policy copies its last command, a copycat form of causal confusion. DAgger with a privileged, safety-gated supervisor gave the first successes but plateaued at 11.1-21.1% across six checkpoints. A map-free runtime shield with a 15 s depth memory, barrier constraints, a cap on motion outside the 73-degree field of view and backoff along the flown path raised the first DAgger policy's success on 180 paired missions from 21.1% to 52.2% (95% CI [45.0, 59.4]; exact McNemar p = 1.2 x 10^-10) and cut its crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%, while timeouts rose from 2.8% to 23.3%. All six checkpoints gained 30.0-34.4 percentage points, at mean speeds of 1.16-1.36 m/s. The code (https://github.com/ylee-sling/Aero-VPA), the trained policy (72.6 MB, https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/aero-vpa) and the full benchmark dataset are public.

items.title: Adapting Qwen3 to Tajik from 0.6B to 8B: Lower Text Loss Did Not Mean Better Understanding
items.content: arXiv:2611.06062v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Small LoRA adapters trained on Tajik news and books lowered Qwen3's Tajik text loss at every size we tried, from 0.6B to 8B, by 0.60 to 1.45 nats per token, but none of them improved Tajik reading comprehension where it can be measured. On Belebele the 1.7B and 8B adapters left accuracy unchanged and the 4B adapter lowered it by 3.7 points; at 0.6B the score rose by 4.2 points but sits near chance and coincides with a change in which answer letter the model prefers, so we do not read it as understanding. At 8B, continued pretraining on about 375 million tokens of raw Tajik text was followed by a Belebele gain of 9.9 points. After a further supervised fine-tuning stage, our main model, e3, is 11.4 points above Qwen3-8B on Belebele; its English MMLU changed by -1.2 points, and a loss larger than 3.3 points is excluded. The same heavy recipe applied to Qwen3-0.6B-Base brought its text loss close to that of the 8B model after books-only pretraining, while its multiple-choice answers stayed near chance and its English MMLU fell by 7.6 points. We report 15 trained models and their 5 starting models from June to October 2025, scored in 2026 on one harness with paired intervals, and we report what went wrong: lost training records, a thinking-mode dataset with almost no reasoning in it, later branches whose training data was never documented, and a 4-bit release that contains no transformer layers.
items.author: Tohir Saidzoda, Madina Abdusalomzoda, Nasimjon Rajabov, Akhrorkhon Ikromov, Komron Giyosiev, Abubakr Abdullozoda, Amin Jalilov, Jonibek Kishvarov, Rahmonali Sharipov, Mariyamkhon Shodyeva
items.summary: This paper systematically adapts Qwen3 models (0.6B to 8B) to Tajik with LoRA adapters and continued pretraining, showing that lower Tajik text loss did not translate into better reading comprehension on Belebele at most scales. Continued pretraining on roughly 375M tokens plus supervised fine-tuning yielded a model 11.4 points above Qwen3-8B on Belebele, though with English capability costs. It is a valuable empirical caution for language-adaptation practice.
items.reasoning: Honest, multi-scale empirical study with a widely useful lesson that perplexity gains do not imply comprehension gains; practical but modest novelty in technique.

items.title: Whose Values Are Generated? Measuring Visual Value Leakage in Multilingual Text-to-Image Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.05578v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) systems serve users across languages and cultural contexts. However, evaluations of cultural representation focus mainly on recognizable elements such as landmarks, clothing, and activities, overlooking the cultural values that generated images convey. To bridge this gap, we introduce VisionValueBench, a multilingual benchmark that operationalizes six of Hofstede's cultural value dimensions (e.g., individualism versus collectivism) to investigate how T2I systems frame neutral social situations through a particular cultural orientation. We find that value-neutral prompts, which admit diverse cultural interpretations, nonetheless yield images that favor particular value orientations, a phenomenon we call visual value leakage. We evaluate prompts varying in language and geographic cues across 960 social scenarios and six T2I configurations. Generated images consistently favor the same value orientations across all six dimensions, for example, equality over hierarchy (low power distance), individual autonomy over group obligation (individualism), and enjoyment over restraint (indulgence). Prompt language has limited influence on these orientations, whereas geographic cues shift some dimensions toward the associated cultural values while largely preserving the prevailing orientations. These findings reveal substantial homogeneity in the cultural values conveyed by T2I systems worldwide.
items.author: Zucan Lyu, Binwei Yao, Rheeya Uppaal, Jing Yao, Xiaoyuan Yi, Junjie Hu

The authors find that value-neutral prompts nonetheless yield images favoring specific value orientations, a phenomenon they call visual value leakage. This extends cultural evaluation of T2I beyond landmarks and clothing to underlying values.
items.reasoning: An original and socially meaningful benchmark introducing a new failure mode concept (visual value leakage) with a defensible theoretical grounding in Hofstede dimensions. Benchmark scope and reliance on Hofstede's somewhat contested framework temper the score, but it fills a real gap in T2I fairness evaluation.

items.title: A Feasibility Condition for Confidence-Gated Tiered LLM Inference
items.content: arXiv:2611.05394v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Tiered inference distributes large language model computation across a hierarchy of devices, from on-device and edge hardware to the datacenter, and is increasingly offered as the route to cheaper, lower-latency, and more private serving. Most such systems orchestrate frozen model checkpoints, and most decide what to resolve locally and what to escalate using a confidence signal produced by a forward-deployed model. We give a closed-form condition for when no threshold on that signal makes a tiered cascade worthwhile relative to sending every query to the backstop. Modeling the routing decision as a binary test and separating local from escalation cost through an architecture cost ratio $\kappa$, we derive a feasibility condition bracketed by a signal-free floor, below which a cascade is feasible at any signal quality, and a perfect-signal ceiling, above which none is. Read along the $\kappa$ axis the condition inverts: where local compute is billed, cost binds, matching a recent empirical finding; where it is sunk, on decentralized hardware, feasibility becomes unconditional and signal quality instead sets what the cascade achieves. We turn the condition into three design requirements that existing trained-in primitives satisfy only in isolation, and we propose, as future work, a co-designed architecture and a protocol to test it. The condition and the inversion hold independently of that architecture; they are the paper's contribution.
items.author: Sumit P. Ahuja
items.summary: This paper derives a closed-form condition determining when confidence-gated tiered LLM inference cascades are worthwhile compared to routing all queries to a datacenter backstop. Modeling routing as a binary test with an architecture cost ratio, it gives practitioners a principled way to know when tiered serving cannot deliver savings regardless of threshold choice.
items.reasoning: The theoretical clarity of a closed-form feasibility condition is valuable for practitioners designing tiered serving, but the analysis is narrow in scope and assumes frozen checkpoints and simple confidence signals.

items.title: Whose Transparency is it Anyway? Understanding Generative AI Transparency Needs and Gaps Across Stakeholders
items.content: arXiv:2611.05549v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Transparency has become a central principle in AI governance, yet there is little agreement about what transparency means, for whom, and in what contexts. Drawing on interpretive flexibility within the Social Construction of Technology, this paper examines how different stakeholders understand and experience transparency in generative AI. This study draws from a global survey of 400 end-users, AI builders, and policymakers, complemented by a structured focus group with end-users, grounding the quantitative findings in qualitative insights from the group most underserved by current transparency practice. We present three key findings. First, all three groups share similar understandings of what transparency means and what it should afford, centered on ensuring accuracy and privacy. Second, gaps between the importance of transparency features and their perceived availability are substantially larger for end-users than builders, revealing how power shapes what gets built and who it serves. Only 28% of end-users report that current transparency practices reflect their needs very well, compared to 53% of builders and 49% of policymakers. Third, transparency is situationally constructed, priorities shift with context and task structure, with role-specific frames activating when context demands them and receding when it does not. We argue that meaningful AI transparency requires moving beyond a one-size-fits-all solution, including current emphases on AI disclosure and static documentation, toward pluralistic transparency infrastructures that reflect the needs of diverse users and stakeholders.
items.author: Genevieve Smith, Sahiba Chopra, Natalia Luka, Min Kyung Lee
items.summary: Drawing on a global survey of 400 end-users, AI builders, and policymakers plus focus groups, this study examines how different stakeholders understand transparency in generative AI. Findings indicate shared understandings of what transparency should afford, but systematic gaps in who is actually served by current transparency practice, with end-users most underserved.
items.reasoning: Methodologically grounded social-science research with practical governance relevance, but the abstracted findings are somewhat predictable and the impact depends on uptake by policy communities.

items.title: Self-Supervised Pretraining for Label-Efficient Facial Expression Recognition using Smart Glasses
items.content: arXiv:2611.05711v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Facial Expression Recognition (FER) on optomyographic (OMG) smart glasses such as OCOsense enables privacy-preserving, camera-free affect sensing for health and well-being. Most FER systems are fully supervised, i.e., they rely either on hand-crafted expert features with classical machine learning, or on end-to-end deep models trained from labelled data. Both depend on large quantities of labelled expressions, which are costly to collect and limit deployment in real-world, personalized settings. We investigate Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) as a route to label-efficient FER on these glasses. We pretrain a Vision Transformer with a masked-autoencoder objective on unlabelled OCOsense recordings and finetune it for five-class FER under person-independent cross-validation. Across label budgets from 5% to 100%, pretraining consistently improves performance; with only 5% of the labels, the pretrained model outperforms the from-scratch model trained with all labels. Our results show that SSL pretraining is a practical way to reduce labelling cost for smart eyewear FER, and we discuss the implications for future personalization and continual adaptation.
items.author: Zhengtao Gao, Francesco Bombassei De Bona, Leonardo Alchieri, Ivana Kiprijanovska, Simon Stankoski, Bojan Sofronievski, Hristijan Gjoreski, Marc Langheinrich, Martin Gjoreski
items.summary: The paper applies masked-autoencoder self-supervised pretraining on optomyographic signals from smart glasses for camera-free, privacy-preserving facial expression recognition, finetuning under personalized few-label settings. It shows SSL can reduce dependence on costly labelled expression data. Relevant to wearable health and affective computing applications.
items.reasoning: Solid application of established SSL techniques to a novel sensing modality with practical privacy benefits, but the methodology is largely a transfer of known approaches rather than a fundamentally new technique.

items.title: From Handcrafted to Generative: RLVR-Optimized Icon Generation for Alexa+
items.content: arXiv:2611.06123v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Alexa+ devices with screens display animated icons during conversations to visually reinforce what is being said. The original set of these icons was hand-drawn by designers one at a time, a process that produces polished results but is time-consuming and cannot scale to the range of topics encountered in open-ended conversation. We describe an automated pipeline, deployed in production, that generates these vectorised animated icons from a text description alone and surfaces relevant animations to customers based on their ongoing conversation. The pipeline decomposes icon creation into a sequence of stages (image generation, semantic decomposition, vectorisation, styling, and animation). Its quality is determined at the very first of these, image generation, on which every downstream stage depends. We therefore focus on improving this first and most critical stage. Because the icons are rendered on small display canvases under strict design guidelines, generations are often unsuitable for production. Supervised fine-tuning is not viable, as no dataset of line-art icons exists under these constraints. Instead, we design objective verifiers that automatically flag generations violating the design guidelines, and use them to fine-tune a flow matching image generation model via reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR). The fine-tuned model raises the pass rate from 15.7% to 58.7% (3.7x) under a VLM judge that is independent of the reward model. Both the trained model and the verifier are deployed in the production pipeline, where the verifier also serves as the automated quality gate before final design review.
items.author: Rohan Sequeira, Matthew Rosenberg, Amin Mahmoudabadbozchelou, Oleg Poliannikov, Jonathan Rubin
items.summary: Describes a production pipeline from Amazon that automatically generates vectorized animated icons for Alexa+ devices from text descriptions, replacing hand-drawn assets. The pipeline stages include image generation, semantic decomposition, vectorisation, styling, and animation, with quality optimized via RL with verifiable rewards.
items.reasoning: Notable as a deployed industrial application of RLVR to generative asset creation, though it is an applied system paper with limited generalizable methodology.

The original set of these icons was hand-drawn by designers one at a time, a process that produces polished results but is time-consuming and cannot scale to the range of topics encountered in open-ended conversation. We describe an automated pipeline, deployed in production, that generates these vectorised animated icons from a text description alone and surfaces relevant animations to customers based on their ongoing conversation. The pipeline decomposes icon creation into a sequence of stages (image generation, semantic decomposition, vectorisation, styling, and animation). Its quality is determined at the very first of these, image generation, on which every downstream stage depends. We therefore focus on improving this first and most critical stage. Because the icons are rendered on small display canvases under strict design guidelines, generations are often unsuitable for production. Supervised fine-tuning is not viable, as no dataset of line-art icons exists under these constraints. Instead, we design objective verifiers that automatically flag generations violating the design guidelines, and use them to fine-tune a flow matching image generation model via reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR). The fine-tuned model raises the pass rate from 15.7% to 58.7% (3.7x) under a VLM judge that is independent of the reward model. Both the trained model and the verifier are deployed in the production pipeline, where the verifier also serves as the automated quality gate before final design review.

items.title: EviSeek: An Evidence-Centric Agentic Framework for Embodied Active Information Seeking
items.content: arXiv:2611.06434v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Active embodied question answering requires agents to acquire evidence through viewpoint changes and physical interaction. The central challenge is to avoid undirected interaction: taking plausible actions without specifying what evidence they should reveal for answering the question. Action plans and accumulated histories alone can leave the informational purpose of an interaction implicit. We introduce EviSeek, a training-free framework that makes question-derived evidence demands explicit acquisition objectives, linking observation-conditioned actions and selectively retained evidence to the information the agent seeks. On 3,436 ESI-Bench questions, EviSeek improves accuracy over the Single-model agent by 7.1 percentage points with Qwen3-VL-32B and 3.7 points with Gemini 3.1 Pro, while improving visual-support-weighted accuracy and reducing mean token usage. These findings support making the informational purpose of interaction explicit, with action selection and evidence retention organized around what the agent needs to learn to answer the question.

items.title: Rules, Traces and Routing Statistics: Training and Calibration Data for Open Models on ARC-AGI-2
items.content: arXiv:2611.06827v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We study which training and calibration data help three open models solve ARC-AGI-2 tasks when the solver runs offline on four L4 GPUs for at most 12 hours. We compare data offline on public tasks and report 189 runs on the 120 hidden semi-private tasks. For the NVARC Qwen3-4B grid model, we built a corpus of 12,000 executable rules in a typed language and 95,993 tasks; a rule is admitted only if its behaviour on a fixed probe set differs from that of every admitted rule, and a task only if its pairs refute a shortlist of nearest competing rules and defeat 12 shortcut solvers. Continued fine-tuning on 1,920 real task records with revised four-GPU scheduling raised the semi-private score from 28.96 (mean of the released model) to 33.06 (mean of five runs, best 34.86); no checkpoint trained with synthetic tasks, even all 95,993 of them, improved on the real-task model. For the Qwen3.8-27B reasoning model, we fine-tuned on 1,036 of its own reasoning traces with correct final answers and compared sets that add traces of other models and synthetic tasks. With an inference procedure built around the model (a thinking cap enforced in the serving engine, a Python program checked on the demonstrations after each answer, a long first attempt per input), the score rose from 26.81 to 44.03, the level the ARC Prize Foundation measured for the base model without a time limit (42.36); most of the gain came from the inference procedure. For the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next mixture-of-experts model (125B parameters, 6B active), GPU memory limited concurrency. Pruning from 512 to 384 experts per layer by router-weighted activation saliency grew the key-value cache from 0.55M to 1.39M tokens; a 296-expert list adapted with ARC routing statistics, keeping experts for program tokens, plus an FP8 indexer cache, reached 1.96M. With a tool that checks programs, the model scored 56.67, our best result.

items.title: Hallucination Is Linearly Decodable from Mid-Layer Hidden States in Quantized LLMs
items.content: arXiv:2606.02628v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We investigate whether open-source LLMs encode a linearly separable truthfulness signal in their hidden states, and at which network depth this signal is strongest. Across three $7$B--$8$B instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B) loaded in $4$-bit NF4 quantization, we extract per-layer hidden states on four hallucination benchmarks (TruthfulQA, HaluEval-QA, FEVER, and a controlled synthetic set) and compare four detection approaches: linear and MLP probes, INSIDE EigenScore, self-consistency, and attention entropy. A linear probe on a single mid-network layer achieves $0.904$--$1.000$ AUROC on held-out splits, while sampling-based detectors do not exceed $0.541$ AUROC under the same protocol. The truthfulness signal is approximately linear: MLP probes rarely surpass linear probes by more than $0.01$ AUROC. Peak probing layers fall in a consistent band across model families on natural-language benchmarks -- blocks~$13$--$18$ of~$32$ for Llama and Mistral, and blocks~$19$--$25$ of~$28$ for Qwen. First-block attention entropy provides a complementary signal in knowledge-grounded settings ($0.866$--$0.941$ AUROC on HaluEval-QA) at no additional inference cost. The low discriminability of sampling methods under this protocol reflects a structural mismatch between paired-label evaluation and the information these methods access, rather than an inherent limitation of those methods. Code and data are released for full reproducibility on a single $8$\,GB GPU.

It characterizes where truthfulness signals are linearly decodable in quantized models across four hallucination benchmarks. This supports cheap, internal hallucination detection for deployed models.

items.title: Constraint-Preserving Flow Matching for Spectral Graph Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.05436v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Spectral graph generation models graphs through the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of their Laplacians, providing a compact and continuous alternative to direct graph construction. However, these eigensystems must retain the structural properties of graph Laplacians. Existing approaches preserve eigenvector orthonormality but do not enforce the Laplacian nullspace constraint, potentially producing eigensystems inconsistent with Laplacian structure. To address this, we introduce Laplacian-Constrained Stiefel Flow Matching (LaSFM), which preserves the nullspace condition alongside eigenvector orthonormality and positive eigenvalues during generation. We characterize the underlying constrained Stiefel manifold and formulate flow matching on it. We further extend LaSFM to property-guided generation, steering samples toward desired graph properties while maintaining these constraints. Experiments demonstrate improved performance on both spectral and graph-level metrics, along with better alignment with target properties.
items.author: Anita Yang, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, Yohan Jung
items.summary: LaSFM formulates flow matching on the Stiefel manifold to generate spectral graph representations that provably preserve Laplacian structure: eigenvector orthonormality, positive eigenvalues, and the nullspace constraint that prior methods ignore. This yields eigensystems consistent with actual graph Laplacians.
items.reasoning: Technically solid contribution combining constrained manifold flow matching with spectral graph generation, fixing a real structural flaw in prior work. The topic is fairly specialized in graph generative modeling, limiting breadth of impact.

items.title: Whiel: A Neurosymbolic Platform for Certified Relational Program Verification
items.content: arXiv:2611.05612v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We present the Whiel (a contraction of Whi(le-R)el) system for Lean-certified reasoning about imperative relational programs. The system can encode containment and equivalence problems for Datalog, its extensions with negation, and the core fragment of graph query languages. It can also represent optimized or incremental evaluation algorithms that are not expressible in the original query language, as well as first-order specifications of integrity constraints, schema mappings, and views arising in data integration, exchange, and sharing. Whiel's program states are database instances, and its imperative structure enables compositional Hoare-style reasoning with first-order relational specifications, using prophecy variables and leveled invariants to support inductive arguments. Whiel supports neurosymbolic discovery of loop invariants whose verification conditions can be checked using the Vampire first-order theorem prover. Counterexamples are fed back into the neurosymbolic pipeline, while proposed solutions are translated into Lean proof certificates. To validate the Whiel system, we evaluate its performance on a curated benchmark suite. In summary, we envision the Whiel system as a tool for tackling mathematically demanding, typically undecidable problems involving complex query and constraint languages, with a high degree of trust in its output.

items.title: Text-Only Domain Adaptation for Low-Resource Medical ASR: Shallow Fusion and Density Ratio Rescoring for Hausa
items.content: arXiv:2611.05744v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems often struggle with specialised medical vocabulary, especially in low-resource languages where domain-specific speech data are scarce. We investigate text-only domain adaptation for Hausa medical ASR using the fixed MMS-1B-FL102 acoustic model and two decoding-time language-model fusion methods: Shallow Fusion (SF) and the Density Ratio Approach (DRA). A 4-gram KenLM trained on 19,421 Hausa health sentences serves as the medical target model, while a 75,372-sentence general-domain model provides the source prior for DRA. Evaluation uses 250 recordings of 25 physician-reviewed prompts from 10 speakers across six northern Nigerian states. Under prompt-disjoint five-fold cross-validation, SF and DRA reduce WER from 29.56% to 23.55% and 23.33%, respectively. Both significantly outperform greedy decoding (p < 0.001), while their difference is not significant (p = 0.423). However, general-LM-only SF achieves 23.96% WER, indicating that the medical LM's additional improvement over a general LM is modest. Medical Term Error Rate also improves under fusion, but does not establish a distinct medical-domain advantage. These findings demonstrate that lightweight, text-only language-model fusion can improve Hausa medical ASR without additional domain-specific speech collection.

items.summary: This paper adapts a fixed MMS-1B-FL102 acoustic model to Hausa medical speech recognition using only text data, comparing shallow fusion and density ratio rescoring with KenLM language models built from medical and general-domain corpora. Evaluation uses physician-reviewed recordings from ten speakers across six northern Nigerian states under prompt-disjoint cross-validation. It demonstrates a practical recipe for low-resource, domain-specific ASR without new speech data collection.

items.title: Clips2Story: Training-Free Video Storyboarding and Editing Using Multimodal Retrieval-Embedded Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.05992v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Video editors often work with large collections of fragmented footage and must select and organize relevant clips into a coherent story. However, many existing video editing and summarization methods assume a temporally ordered source video and aim to preserve its original narrative and temporal structure. In this paper, we introduce Clips2Story, a training-free, LLM-based pipeline that enables users to create keyword-specified short videos from a pool of video clips. Given a pool of clips and a user-specified keyword, we first extract text-based multimodal descriptors for each clip and retrieve the clips most relevant to the keyword. We then provide the textual descriptors of these candidate clips to an LLM, which selects and arranges them into an editable storyboard with connective narrations. Finally, we assemble the selected clips and retrieve accompanying visuals for the narrations to compose the output video. To evaluate the proposed pipeline, we construct a synthetic evaluation dataset from 100 long-form videos across five genres by segmenting each video into short clips using a scene-change detection model and shuffling the resulting clips to remove their temporal order. Through objective evaluation and qualitative examples, we demonstrate that Clips2Story can effectively retrieve keyword-relevant clips and compose coherent storyboards based on user-specified keywords. Human evaluation further shows that Clips2Story outperforms a strong baseline in terms of narrative coherence, keyword alignment, and overall realism.

It addresses a real gap, since most video editing tools assume a single temporally ordered source video.

items.title: Today's Work, Tomorrow's Workforce: Incentivizing Learning in AI-Assisted Work
items.content: arXiv:2611.06346v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: At work, people develop skills through experience: novices acquire skills by completing tasks, while experts retain theirs through continued practice. AI assistance changes this process by offering workers a choice between solving tasks independently and accepting the AI's answers. While relying on AI saves immediate effort, it can also displace the practice needed to acquire and retain skills, including those required to oversee the AI. We extend an existing accept-or-solve model to a sequence of tasks in which workers' skills evolve through independent practice and reliance on AI. We compare myopic workers, who maximize immediate utility, with strategic workers, who also value their future skills. We show that novices can become trapped at low skill levels, while experts may lose skill, even as AI-assisted outcome accuracy remains high. Strategic workers, by contrast, may choose to solve independently even when AI is more accurate, recognizing the future value of acquiring and retaining their skills. We then study incentives that reward correct independent work and characterize the payments needed to encourage skill acquisition and retention. We show that independent work can become self-sustaining once workers acquire sufficient skill, eliminating the need for continued incentives. Counterintuitively, supporting a higher skill target can sometimes reduce long-run incentive costs, either by enabling self-sustaining independent work or by lowering the payments needed to maintain proficiency. Our findings thereby shift the focus from whether workers should rely on AI on individual tasks to how organizations can sustain human expertise over time, and which skills are worth investing in.
items.author: Moritz Diener, Daniel Hendriks, Philipp Spitzer, Gerhard Satzger, Joshua Holstein, Wei Sun
items.summary: This paper models how AI assistance affects worker skill formation over a sequence of accept-or-solve tasks, comparing myopic workers who maximize immediate utility with strategic workers who value future skills. It shows novices can become trapped in AI reliance, with implications for skill acquisition, retention, and the ability to oversee AI.
items.reasoning: Timely and policy-relevant economic/behavioral modeling of AI dependence and skill atrophy, extending an established model with dynamic skill evolution. The framework is illustrative rather than empirically validated, limiting impact, but the novices-trap finding is an important caution for AI-assisted work design.

items.title: Noise-regularized training of quantum circuit Born machines under a finite shot budget
items.content: arXiv:2611.06630v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Quantum circuit Born machines (QCBMs) can learn distributions that are hard to sample from classically, but their value depends on generalizing from finite training data. Here, we study how hardware noise affects this generalization. We show that, for any noise process, the generalization gap of a QCBM trained with the maximum mean discrepancy is bounded by the complexity of the distributions the noisy model can reach. Scrambled local Pauli noise contracts this complexity but biases the model towards the uniform distribution, so residual noise acts as a regularizer whose optimal strength can be intermediate. We propose GENIE, a framework that realizes a chosen noise level with capped error mitigation and selects it during training from held-out data within a fixed execution budget, with provably bounded regret. In simulations on synthetic and census data, GENIE stays close to the best of four noise-control strategies, whereas every fixed noise level falls short in many settings.

We propose GENIE, a framework that realizes a chosen noise level with capped error mitigation and selects it during training from held-out data within a fixed execution budget, with provably bounded regret. In simulations on synthetic and census data, GENIE stays close to the best of four noise-control strategies, whereas every fixed noise level falls short in many settings.

items.title: Route First, See Later: Enabling Vision Agents to Reason Scientifically by Separating Routing Policy from Action Spaces
items.content: arXiv:2611.06760v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Scientific image-analysis workflows require agents to select among diverse capabilities like description, detection, counting, and segmentation. Current multi-tool architectures conflate intent interpretation with visual execution, masking whether a failure arises from flawed reasoning (misrouting) or failed perception (invalid tool execution). This lack of auditability renders agents unreliable for high-stakes scientific automation. We introduce ZETA, an extensible architecture that operationalizes the decoupling of routing policy from action execution. ZETA resolves scientific intent before invoking specialized visual tools, treating measurement as a deterministic operation grounded in explicit geometry rather than generative output. This architecture exposes the "black box" of agent decision-making, allowing routing correctness and downstream execution to be evaluated as independent failure modes.   To our knowledge, we provide the first controlled study in scientific vision-agent routing that isolates explicit routing-policy specification while holding the legal action interface fixed. Evaluation on a zero-shot benchmark of 51 scientific-intent queries shows that explicit routing semantics can substantially improve routing accuracy, particularly at semantically adjacent action boundaries, although improvements vary across models. For Qwen 3.8, explicit routing-policy specification improves segmentation routing accuracy from 6.2% to 75.0% and detection routing accuracy from 60.0% to 100%. ZETA's execution traces make routing decisions and downstream artifacts separately observable, providing a basis for distinguishing intent-selection errors from visual execution failures. ZETA establishes the necessary infrastructure to isolate execution errors from interpretive ones, a critical requirement for deploying reliable scientific vision agents.

items.title: CounterFactual Retrieval for Evidence-Aware Individual Animal Identification
items.content: arXiv:2611.06864v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Automated identification of individual animals is moving from small curated studies toward shared benchmarks and reusable foundation models. This progress is useful, but current evaluation leaves the evidence behind a match unresolved, i.e., high retrieval accuracy does not show whether a model used animal features or identity-correlated shortcuts. We address this with Counterfactual Foreground Retrieval (CFR), an evidence-aware evaluation protocol. CFR evaluates the same query-gallery task under different views: full image, foreground-only, and shortcut-only. The full-image measures standard retrieval performance; the foreground-only measures foreground-supported retrieval; and shortcut-only view measure how much identity signal is recoverable from background, or silhouette. This turns a retrieval score into an evidence profile: how well the model performs on the original images, how much of that performance remains when only the animal is visible, and how much identity signal remains recoverable when the animal is removed. We release around 0.5M masks for 34 datasets and code for mask generation and CFR evaluation.

items.summary: The paper proposes Counterfactual Forensic Retrieval (CFR), an evidence-aware evaluation protocol for individual animal identification that tests the same query-gallery task under full-image, foreground-only, and shortcut-only views. This reveals whether high retrieval accuracy reflects genuine animal features or identity-correlated shortcuts, addressing a blind spot as wildlife re-identification moves to shared benchmarks and foundation models. It is a methodological contribution to evaluation rigor in computer vision for conservation.

items.title: The Information Limits of Neural Controlled Differential Equations Under Sparse Observations
items.content: arXiv:2611.03887v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Neural controlled differential equations (Neural CDEs) evolve hidden states along continuous paths constructed by interpolating discrete observations. Sparse measurements leave the input between observation times undetermined, and admissible continuous paths consistent with the same data can produce different terminal states. We characterize this ambiguity for planar drivers with bounded speed. The set of compatible terminal states admits a leading-order zonotopic approximation determined by feasible signed areas and transported Lie brackets. Its projection onto a scalar prediction yields a computable, target-specific ambiguity certificate. We also study the number of measurements needed to reduce the remaining uncertainty. For nondegenerate planar CDEs, the optimal worst-case radius over deterministic adaptive sampling policies scales as $N^{-1}$ when speed is bounded and $N^{-2}$ when both speed and acceleration are bounded, where $N$ is the number of observation intervals. Synthetic experiments assess the certificate using admissible continuous completions and examine the role of path regularity.

items.title: P$^2$-MOPD: Accelerating Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation via Parameter Priors
items.content: arXiv:2611.03953v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation consolidates expert capabilities by supervising student-generated trajectories, whereas task arithmetic offers a training-free alternative through linear parameter combinations. We view the linear combination of student and expert parameters as a single differentiable model and propose P$^2$-MOPD, which jointly optimizes the mixing coefficients and the student weights under the same on-policy distillation objective. Unlike task arithmetic, which stays within the span of the frozen student and expert parameters for any choice of merging coefficients, P$^2$-MOPD keeps the student trainable, so the experts act as parameter priors without confining it to this span. Across four domains at 1.7B and 4B scales, P$^2$-MOPD achieves faster and more balanced recovery than MOPD from the same initialization, surpassing its final average recovery in half the training steps. At the end of training, our 1.7B model reaches 94.7% average recovery, versus 80.9% for MOPD.

items.title: One Mistake, Three Layers: Persistence Rules Under Depth Correlation
items.content: arXiv:2611.03968v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Probing frozen representations layer by layer is now standard practice, but reporting when a signal first becomes decodable requires a rule for reading a depth curve, and the obvious rule is wrong. On synthetic curves with known ground truth, requiring a probe score to exceed a null-calibrated threshold for three consecutive stages reports an onset nineteen stages early under transformer-like depth correlation, with every resample returning an onset. The failure follows from correlation between neighboring layers, a hazard known in neuroimaging but not, to our knowledge, checked for depth curves.   We give an estimator whose error rate is calibrated rather than assumed. Null trajectories are built by permuting labels within each evaluation unit and holding each permutation fixed across depth, preserving the correlation structure the rule must survive; thresholds are per-layer order statistics; and the persistence requirement is calibrated rather than chosen.   Applied to pocket information in a frozen co-folding trunk, stratifying 1,820 post-cutoff targets by protein-family and pocket familiarity, the five-stage rule fires on 4 to 7 per cent of null trajectories against a nominal 5 per cent and the three-stage rule on 12 to 17: the synthetic failure reproduces on real data. Pocket membership is decodable above threshold at all 48 blocks in all four regimes, so the onset cannot discriminate them; the pre-declared accumulation depth does, and is latest for familiar families with structurally novel pockets in every feature set. That regime is also the weakest, by a margin surviving controls for length, pocket measure and alignment depth.   Separately, a widely used public co-folding checkpoint loads against its own code with 128 trunk parameters missing; those would be randomly initialized, and every representation extracted would be partly noise while appearing normal.

items.title: Structured Priors: Towards an algebra of component priors for prior-data fitted networks
items.content: arXiv:2611.04056v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Prior-data fitted networks are typically trained using synthetic data generated by a single, manually constructed generator. In cases where such a generator combines multiple components, e.g., in TabPFN, Mitra, or TabICLv2, this is achieved through a mixture using manually specified weights, the impact of which on the network only becomes apparent after pre-training. Instead of such a hand-built generator, this work proposes a structured prior: a small set of named component priors, linked by operators whose algebraic properties are formally proven and whose influence on the trained network has been validated. Within a measure-theoretic framework, the operators of mixture, convolution, amplitude scaling, local transform, and projection are defined. Their governing laws are proven. These operators are implemented in the macl2l software package. Experiments demonstrate that the implemented generators reproduce the identities within the resolution of a permutation test. Furthermore, it is shown that trained networks obey the distributive law; that a mixed prior composed of small components performs as well as or better than any individual component in seven out of eight open regression benchmarks; and that on two of these tables a structured prior reaches, with a ninth of the data budget, an error that a generic random-function prior does not reach even with the full budget. A theorem on model averaging demonstrates that networks trained on individual components constitute the Bayes predictor for the mixture, provided that the component networks are themselves the Bayes predictors for their respective priors. However, the pre-registered test of this averaged predictor with trained component networks failed, because the networks identify the generating component too rarely. The paper proposes a research program focused on the algebra of structured priors for prior-data fitted networks.

items.title: When Strong Reasoners Join the Pool: Small Union Premiums and Costly Runaway Generations in LLM Routing
items.content: arXiv:2611.04098v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Routing benchmarks often judge a router against a hindsight oracle that counts a query as solved whenever any model's recorded answer is correct, but under stochastic decoding that oracle mixes two different objects: the clairvoyant ceiling of committing to one model per query and the premium of calling several models and keeping any correct answer. A companion study measured this premium at 3.5 percentage points (pp) for 11 small open models on MATH-500; how large it is once current reasoning models enter the pool was unknown. We measure it with a fixed-protocol, pre-committed generation on a single NVIDIA B300: all 500 MATH-500 problems, 30 seeded samples per problem, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and NVIDIA's Nemotron Nano 9B v2 and Nemotron Super 49B v1.5 (a NAS derivative of the same 70B) under vendor sampling, a 65,536-token cap, a pinned Math-Verify scorer, and an append-only attempt ledger, for 45,000 scored responses. The two reasoning models both reach 96.1% accuracy against 76.2% for the 70B baseline. The empirical product-coupling premium is 0.215-0.588 pp across all two- and three-model pools; the empirical plug-in selection headroom over always calling Nano is 1.27 pp; and resampling Nano three times gives practically the same empirical any-correct rate as calling all three models once. Only 31 responses reached the cap, 25 of them with exactly periodic tails, yet the capped responses account for up to 60.2% of a model's output-length-squared proxy, and long generations made a fourth planned model, Llama-3.1-8B, too slow to finish. The premium is far below the companion's 3.5 pp, but models, pool size and protocol changed together; an oracle gap should therefore be reported with the pool, the protocol, the samples per cell and the decoding budget that produced it.

items.title: Deep Learning Compilers: Architecture, Optimization, and Empirical Characterization
items.content: arXiv:2611.04273v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: As deep learning (DL) models become increasingly complex and hardware architectures grow more heterogeneous, DL compilers play a critical role in optimizing computational efficiency and enabling scalable deployment. This paper presents a systematic analysis of DL compilers, covering their architectural evolution, compilation workflows, optimization techniques, and emerging research directions. We organize DL compiler architectures into frontend, middle-end, and backend stages, emphasizing the role of the middle-end in connecting high-level model representations with hardware-specific optimizations. We further examine representative DL compilers and recent optimization techniques across different compilation stages. Beyond architectural and technical analysis, we conduct an empirical evaluation of compiler behaviors to investigate the effectiveness of graph optimization, compilation overhead, and dynamic-shape handling. Experiments using PyTorch/TorchInductor on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 demonstrate that compiler benefits depend strongly on workload characteristics, with speedups of up to 8.21\times for fusion-friendly computation graphs, while other workloads exhibit limited improvements. Our results further reveal that compilation overhead can require thousands of executions to amortize, and dynamic-shape compilation reduces cumulative shape-transition costs by approximately 70\% at the expense of modest steady-state performance degradation. By combining systematic architectural analysis with quantitative experimental evidence, this work provides insights into the design, optimization, and practical deployment of modern DL compilers.

items.title: CAPSkip: Cancellation-Aware Prefix Skipping for Selective Backpropagation
items.content: arXiv:2611.04611v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Per-step selective back-propagation forwards every example of a mini-batch but back-propagates only some of them. Most rules rank examples by loss or gradient magnitude, but such scalar scores ignore cancellation between per-example gradients: the gradient removed by a set can be much smaller than its individual magnitudes suggest. We introduce CAPSkip (Cancellation-Aware Prefix Skipping). Among the examples the model already classifies correctly, CAPSkip skips the longest prefix, in increasing order of last-layer gradient norm, whose vector sum stays within a relative budget $b$ of the batch's last-layer gradient. In exact arithmetic this bounds the change of the raw final-layer gradient, using rank-one contributions already available from the forward pass; the bound does not extend to deeper layers, optimizer updates, or the training trajectory. Because the cumulative distortion is not monotone in the prefix length, CAPSkip scans all prefixes; a factorised Gram matrix makes the scan cheap and keeps it on the device. With activation reuse and selected-row backward, CAPSkip fine-tunes DeiT-S on CIFAR-100 for 103 epochs in 0.576x the time of 103-epoch dense training, and is +0.25 pp [+0.08, +0.42] above an approximately time-matched 59-epoch dense run (n=3).
items.author: Heejin Choi
items.summary: CAPSkip improves selective backpropagation by accounting for cancellation between per-example gradients, which scalar scores like loss or gradient magnitude ignore. Among correctly classified examples, it skips the longest prefix in increasing last-layer gradient-norm order whose vector sum stays within a relative budget of the batch gradient, bounding the change to the raw final-layer gradient in exact arithmetic. This enables cheaper training with a controlled effect on the update.
items.reasoning: A clever, well-motivated efficiency idea grounded in the structure of gradient cancellation, with a clean bounded-change guarantee. However, it is limited to final-layer gradients in its exact form and addresses a somewhat narrow efficiency niche (selective backprop), so broad impact is uncertain.

items.title: Leakage-free evaluation of residual graph convolutional networks for network intrusion detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.04660v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Graph neural networks are increasingly proposed for network intrusion detection, yet many reported results come from protocols in which test flows shape the graph used for training, duplicated flows sit on both sides of the split, or a single split is reported. This study measures what a residual graph convolutional network gains over simpler models once these sources of optimism are removed. CICIDS2017 and NF-UNSW-NB15-v2 were cleaned with label-aware removal of exact duplicates, removing 69% of NF-UNSW-NB15-v2 flows. Flows were linked in a nearest-neighbour graph built from training flows only, and validation and test flows were attached to their nearest training flows at prediction time. A two-layer residual network was compared with eight models under the same settings, including a nearest-neighbour vote over the same graph, gradient-boosted trees and a random forest, over three seeds that each draw a new split, with ablations, leave-one-family-out and feature-noise tests. On CICIDS2017 the residual network reached a binary F1 of 98.11% (SD 0.18) and on NF-UNSW-NB15-v2 90.57% (0.38), indistinguishable from a multilayer perceptron without the graph and from other graph networks. Tree ensembles were 1.48 to 1.57 F1 points higher on CICIDS2017 and led on the area under the precision-recall curve on both datasets; their CICIDS2017 multiclass macro-F1 reached 93.08% against 64.51%, a gap mainly from benign flows the residual network assigned to small attack classes. No ablation, including transductive graph construction, changed F1 beyond seed variation. Under Gaussian feature noise (SD 0.5), the residual network kept an F1 of 96.16%, while XGBoost fell to 0.67%. Under a leakage-controlled protocol, message passing over flow graphs adds no measurable accuracy over a perceptron, and tree ensembles remain stronger on both; the advantage of graph models lies in robustness to feature noise.
items.author: Zahid Iqbal
items.summary: This paper audits common data-leakage pitfalls in graph-based network intrusion detection, where test flows contaminate the training graph, duplicates straddle splits, and only single splits are reported. After rigorous label-aware deduplication (removing 69% of flows in NF-UNSW-NB15-v2) and train-only graph construction, a two-layer residual GCN is compared against simpler baselines. The work matters because it quantifies how much of the reported advantage of GNNs in this domain may be evaluation optimism rather than genuine capability.
items.reasoning: Methodologically valuable negative/replication-style work exposing inflated results in an applied subfield; the leakage-aware evaluation protocol is useful for the community, but the contribution is corrective rather than architecturally novel and is confined to two benchmark datasets.

items.title: TAPES: Task-Aligned Joint Predictive Pretraining for Transaction Event Sequences
items.content: arXiv:2611.04747v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Transaction event sequences support diverse prediction tasks in online commerce and digital financial services. The same transaction records can yield prediction targets with different semantics, including values, changes, and relations to past events. These targets impose different constraints on history representations, but their predictability alone does not establish the downstream utility of a target set. Moreover, target-wise prediction losses do not explicitly model conditional co-occurrence among targets. To address these challenges, we propose TAPES, a task-aligned joint predictive pretraining framework for transaction sequences. TAPES constructs a finite collection of candidate target sets from admissible field-operator combinations. It selects a target set according to the downstream utility of representations learned through short joint pretraining trials under matched budgets. It then reinitializes the encoder and pretrains it on the selected targets through a joint likelihood parameterized by a shared discrete latent variable, before downstream supervised adaptation. Experiments in a real-world transaction-risk setting and on multiple public financial benchmarks spanning diverse downstream tasks demonstrate that TAPES outperforms representative baselines. Ablation studies further validate the contributions of predictive target selection and joint modeling.
items.author: Ruobing Zuo, Weiyu Han, Huilin He, Haoyu Jiang, Ze Zhao, Jie Sheng, Xiao Tan, Shuai Chen, Tianyi Zhang
items.summary: TAPES is a pretraining framework for transaction event sequences in online commerce and financial services that constructs candidate target sets from admissible field-operator combinations and performs task-aligned joint prediction, explicitly modeling conditional co-occurrence among prediction targets. This addresses the mismatch between generic predictive pretraining objectives and the diverse downstream semantics (values, changes, relations) of real transaction tasks. It could improve representation quality for industrial sequence models.
items.reasoning: Thoughtful task-aligned objective design grounded in the practical demands of transaction modeling, with a principled treatment of target set selection. Impact depends on deployment evidence not visible in the abstract; the setting is domain-specific.

items.title: Attending to Memory Writes Reduces Seed Variability in Recurrent Length Generalization
items.content: arXiv:2611.04902v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recurrent memory requires learning useful updates, but attention added to assist learning can also compromise length generalization. We study bounded delta attention: causal attention over uncorrected update proposals whose bounded correction enters the recurrent update. Its implementation in TraceRelay combines additive phase recurrence with attention computed before a parallel scan. On prefix-supervised modulo-5, trained at lengths 1--40, three findings characterize its behavior at length 80. First, upper delta attention attains $70.81\pm8.26$% accuracy across seven seeds, versus $69.21\pm22.42$% for the local-attention recurrent baseline (mean $\pm$ sample SD): a 63.2% reduction in SD with a similar mean. Upper state attention also reduces variation, reaching $74.75\pm6.24$%, so this benefit is not unique to update-level attention. Disabling the upper delta correction retains $70.62\pm8.60$%. Second, blocking gradients at the delta-attention inputs changes accuracy to $65.25\pm12.40$% in the matched seven-seed comparison, increasing SD by 50.2%. It also delays a 99% validation threshold on average among the same six seeds that reach it; the 95% threshold is reached earlier on average with input-gradient blocking across all seven seeds. Third, lower delta attention exhibits substantially less extrapolation degradation than lower state attention: 62.60% versus 19.40%, against a 71.06% baseline. Removing its correction reduces accuracy to 22.56%; its advantage over lower state attention also persists under input-gradient blocking. These observations motivate bounded update-level attention as a recurrent learning scaffold, combining reduced seed variation with less severe degradation in a placement where state attention fails.
items.author: Sungwoo Goo, Hwi-yeol Yun, Sangkeun Jung
items.summary: The paper studies bounded delta attention in recurrent memory models, implemented in TraceRelay with additive phase recurrence and attention computed before a parallel scan. On prefix-supervised modulo-5 tasks trained at lengths 1-40 and tested at length 80, upper delta attention achieves similar mean accuracy to a local-attention recurrent baseline but with dramatically reduced seed variance (a 63 percent reduction in standard deviation). The findings suggest attending to memory writes stabilizes length generalization.
items.reasoning: An interesting mechanistic finding connecting attention over memory updates with training stability and length generalization, a topic relevant to recurrent and state-space models. Scope is limited to synthetic algorithmic tasks, capping broader significance.

items.title: DRAP: Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity for Continual Learning in Physical AI
items.content: arXiv:2611.05029v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small per-step policy errors can accumulate over a trajectory. Each deviation may move the agent outside the training distribution, increase subsequent prediction errors, and ultimately cause closed-loop task failure. This work introduces Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP), a replay-free method that estimates the historical importance of adaptable model tensors from sample-level action gradients weighted by local trajectory-amplification risk. A ridge-regularized local linear model is fitted to expert state-action transitions, and the largest singular value of its state-transition matrix provides a policy-independent, Lyapunov-inspired estimate of one-step perturbation amplification. After each task, risk-weighted squared gradients are accumulated in a tensor-level importance memory. During subsequent tasks, DRAP uses normalized cumulative importance to scale the effective AdamW learning rate of each tensor, immediately reducing the plasticity of components that supported previous behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory points. We instantiate DRAP on a fixed KappaTune-selected subnetwork of OpenVLA and evaluate replay-free sequential adaptation across the LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites. Compared with standard AdamW fine-tuning and EWC, the results show substantially improved retention of previously learned behaviors while preserving strong new-suite acquisition.
items.author: Oswaldo Ludwig
items.summary: DRAP is a replay-free continual learning method for physical AI that estimates per-parameter importance from action gradients weighted by a Lyapunov-inspired trajectory-amplification risk, addressing error accumulation in closed-loop control. A ridge-regularized local model fitted to expert transitions yields a policy-independent stability estimate used to modulate plasticity.
items.reasoning: Addressing compounding distribution shift in continual learning for embodied agents is a meaningful, underexplored angle, and the Lyapunov-inspired risk weighting is novel; however, the paper is single-authored with limited apparent empirical breadth from the abstract.

items.title: Going Deeper With Memories
items.content: arXiv:2611.05255v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Byte level language models avoid tokenizer dependence and provide universal coverage, but processing every byte at full resolution is expensive. We introduce DeepMem, a causal multiscale architecture that separates semantic compression from exact byte preservation. A learned invertible subband transform constructs a hierarchy of shorter sequences, while a lossless carrier and explicit detail sidebands preserve byte identity. Fast weight memory blocks operate along the encoder, with iterative shared state computation at the compressed bottleneck, while an attention based super resolution decoder restores byte resolution representations. DeepMem achieves stronger language modeling performance than a matched byte level Transformer on FineWeb-Edu and PG19, and obtains the best macro average performance across the evaluated FLORES languages. It also improves PIQA accuracy while remaining competitive on code modeling, multiple choice reasoning, and byte level corruption robustness. Bottleneck refinement requires approximately $7{,}600\times$ fewer counted FLOPs than equivalent full resolution reasoning, while maintaining competitive evaluation throughput.
items.author: Afshin Khadangi
items.summary: DeepMem is a causal multiscale byte-level language model that separates semantic compression from exact byte preservation using an invertible subband transform, fast-weight memory blocks, and an attention-based super-resolution decoder. It reportedly outperforms a matched byte-level Transformer on FineWeb-Edu while avoiding tokenizer dependence. This is a novel architecture addressing the cost of full-resolution byte processing.
items.reasoning: Creative architecture combining several ideas (multiscale transforms, fast weights, lossless sidebands) with promising results, but it is a single-author paper and empirical evidence is limited to one benchmark; replication uncertainty reduces confidence.

items.title: Aligning Language Models with General Preferences: An Empirical Study of Direct Nash Optimization
items.content: arXiv:2611.05373v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Direct Nash Optimization (DNO) aligns a language model to a general preference function by approximating the Nash equilibrium of a two-player preference game. Its practical variant, DNO-Prct, iterates on-policy sampling, LLM-based rating of the samples together with a teacher's gold response, large-margin preference-pair selection and a DPO-style contrastive update. We re-implement DNO-Prct independently and study it on two open-weight instruct models, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and Mistral 7B Instruct v0.1, with GPT-4o or a larger open-weight model of the same family as the annotator. On AlpacaEval 2.0 with GPT-4o as judge, three iterations raise the length-controlled (LC) win rate against GPT-4o from 31.7% to 45.3% for Llama and from 6.8% to 18.4% for Mistral, and the tuned 8B model scores above Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on every reported win rate. With same-family open-weight annotators, the runs retain 62% (Llama) and 82% (Mistral) of the LC gain achieved with GPT-4o as annotator, so the rating step does not require a proprietary model. In a separate ablation configuration, variants that remove the gold responses, remove the data look-back, or accept only teacher-preferred pairs score 6 to 10 LC points below the full procedure, whereas varying the number of on-policy samples per prompt (1 to 7) moves the LC win rate by at most 2.1 points, and a margin sweep (1 to 5) run in its own pipeline by at most 2.4 points. We also report the cost of the pipeline and where the practical algorithm departs from the theory it approximates. All results are single runs, and GPT-4o is both the teacher and the evaluation judge; we discuss what this implies for the reported gains.
items.author: Austin Tsai, Saurav Nanda, Ganapathy Parthasarathy, Bhuvnesh Kumar, Parivesh Choudhary
items.summary: The authors independently re-implement Direct Nash Optimization (DNO-Prct), an alignment method that finds Nash equilibria of preference games via on-policy sampling, LLM rating, and DPO-style updates, and evaluate it on Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and Mistral 7B Instruct with GPT-4o as annotator. Three iterations raise AlpacaEval 2.0 length-controlled win rates substantially for both models. This provides a useful empirical validation and characterization of a Nash-based alternative to RLHF/DPO pipelines.
items.reasoning: Independent replication of a preference-optimization method with solid empirical gains, but the method was proposed elsewhere and the study mostly confirms rather than fundamentally extends it; both base models are established, not newly released.

items.title: Complete Donor-Set Guidance for Frozen Diffusion Docking Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.03731v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Metalloprotein docking requires a ligand pose to satisfy both global pocket fit and the identity and geometry of metal-coordinating atoms. General-purpose diffusion docking models do not explicitly condition generation on externally specified complete ligand donor sets, and their predicted poses can exhibit incorrect metal-donor relationships. Metal-aware models address coordination during training and generation; here we ask whether external donor information can correct already-trained general-purpose models without retraining. We propose Complete-Identity Contract Guidance (CICG), which applies a supplied complete donor set through translation, rotation, and torsion updates, and Historical Contract Transfer (HCT), which supplies donor identities from earlier complexes at compatible receptor sites. We compare HCT with trajectory-local controls retaining the historical donor count with or without elemental composition. On 86 assessable HCT-covered queries, HCT-guided CICG increases frozen-confidence-selected joint success from 21.5% to 36.6% on SurfDock and from 25.0% to 34.9% on DiffDock-L. The joint criterion requires correct global ligand placement, complete native donor recovery, coordination geometry, preserved stereochemistry, and absence of fatal receptor clashes. Composition-matched guidance reaches 33.14% and 34.30%, leaving the additional benefit of fixed historical membership unresolved. Our results therefore support donor-set guidance as a conditional correction for frozen docking models, while identifying donor-source reliability and physical-quality preservation as the main barriers to broader use.
items.author: Hyunwoo Kim, Insoo Park, Ziseok Lee, Wooyeol Lee, Yoorim Gang, Kyungsu Kim
items.summary: The paper proposes Complete-Identity Contract Guidance (CICG) and Historical Contract Transfer (HCT) to inject metal-coordination donor-set constraints into already-trained general-purpose diffusion docking models without retraining. By applying translation, rotation, and torsion updates guided by a supplied complete donor set, the method corrects metal-donor geometry errors in ligand pose predictions for metalloproteins. This offers a training-free route to metal-aware molecular docking.
items.reasoning: Practical and elegantly scoped: fixing a known failure mode of diffusion docking models via inference-time guidance is valuable for structure-based drug design. Impact is bounded by the niche application area and dependence on external donor-set availability.

items.title: LaplaceDiag: Fault Diagnosis through Changes in Learned Actuator Effects
items.content: arXiv:2611.03849v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Identifying faulty components from sensor anomalies is difficult because fault effects can propagate through a plant and different faults can produce similar observations. Detailed component models and labeled fault examples may also be unavailable. We introduce LaplaceDiag, a data-driven method that uses changes in actuator effects to narrow the search for faulty equipment. Actuators act on specific devices and mechanisms, so their changed effects can provide clues to root causes. LaplaceDiag learns a healthy plant model with LaplaceNet, a neural network that operates in Laplace space. It separates nonlinear prediction based on measured history from an explicit matrix that describes how actuator values affect sensor values. Keeping the history predictor fixed allows current actuator effects to be estimated by linear regression without retraining the neural network. Comparison with a healthy reference accounts for estimation uncertainty and normal variation to detect changes and generate actuator-related diagnostic hypotheses. The method supports online and offline diagnosis, providing an intermediate step between anomaly detection and identifying faulty components. We successfully evaluate LaplaceDiag on two datasets.

items.title: The Complexity of ReLU Network Synthesis from a Parameter Multiset
items.content: arXiv:2611.04074v2 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We ask how hard it is to build a ReLU network when its parameter values are given in advance. An instance supplies an appropriate encoding of a target behavior, a multiset of rational numbers, and a bound on the number of neurons (output included). The question is whether one can choose the graph of a ReLU network within the bound, and place the numbers on its edges and biases so that it meets the target. This separates the numbers from the architecture. Matching two labeled examples exactly is already $\mathsf{NP}$-complete, so we ask what changes when the target must hold on every input or on average. Agreeing with a Boolean circuit on every Boolean input is $\Sigma_2^{\mathsf P}$-complete, already for four neurons. Agreeing with a given ReLU network on every real input lies in $\mathsf{DP}$ for every fixed neuron bound and is $\mathsf{DP}$-complete for three neurons. Approximating a ReLU network on the unit cube within absolute error one everywhere is $\Sigma_2^{\mathsf P}$-complete, even with no hidden neurons and all numbers equal and positive. Deciding whether some network has expected squared loss at most a threshold is $\mathsf{NP}^{\mathsf{PP}}$-complete for uniform Boolean inputs. For uniform inputs on the unit cube and for standard Gaussian inputs with a positive threshold, the same holds for two neurons when a positive risk gap, given in binary and possibly exponentially small, separates yes from no instances. Without a gap, the cube version is complete for guessing a polynomial-length string, then comparing a sum of exponentially many rationals with a threshold, all computable in polynomial time from the input and the guess.
items.author: Dimitrios Myrisiotis
items.summary: The paper studies the computational complexity of constructing a ReLU network when its parameter values are given as a multiset of rationals and only the architecture may be chosen. It proves that exact matching of two examples is NP-complete, while agreement with a Boolean circuit on all inputs is Sigma-2-P-complete even with four neurons, separating the roles of weights and architecture.
items.reasoning: Rigorous theoretical contribution clarifying where hardness lies in network synthesis, which is interesting for expressivity and complexity theory. However, its practical impact on mainstream ML is limited; value is primarily to the theory community.

items.title: How Risky Is Your Data-Driven Policy?
items.content: arXiv:2611.04292v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Data-driven algorithms are ubiquitous across industries, and there is an extensive literature on analyzing their \emph{average} performance. The risk profile of such algorithms, while critical, is much less understood. This paper quantifies the risk of data-driven policies and isolates its sources. We evaluate a policy through the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of its loss over the training sample, any policy randomization, and the future outcome, at a fixed unknown distribution. Regret against an oracle that knows the distribution decomposes into expected post-sample regret (PS), the average outcome-only CVaR gap of the selected action, and a sample-risk premium (SR), the additional tail risk omitted by averaging those evaluations. The analogous premium vanishes under expected loss.   We characterize when the premium vanishes and how large it is relative to post-sample regret. For losses with a continuous density near the tail cutoff, we identify conditions under which both components decay at the same rate, yet the limiting ratio of the premium to post-sample regret can reach the thousands. When a probability mass at the cutoff moves with the action, the premium can decay more slowly and dominate post-sample regret. We establish conditions under which sample average approximation learns the oracle action at rate $n^{-1/2}$ in both settings, but its combined-risk regret is of order $n^{-1}$ in the first and $n^{-1/2}$ in the second. In finite-sample numerical examples of SAA in both settings, the premium accounts for approximately $74\%$--$97\%$ of regret.

items.summary: This paper quantifies the tail risk of data-driven policies using conditional value-at-risk over training samples, policy randomization, and future outcomes. It decomposes regret against a distribution-knowing oracle into expected post-sample regret and a sample-risk premium capturing tail risk omitted by average-case analysis.
items.reasoning: Addresses an underexplored and important question, the risk profile rather than average performance of learned policies, with a clean theoretical decomposition. Authors are credible (operations research/statistical learning), but the framework is abstract and its adoption in ML practice is uncertain.

items.title: One-shot Distributed Learning via Weighted Averaging with Server-side Information
items.content: arXiv:2611.04700v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Distributed learning has drawn considerable attention due to its capability of learning from distributed data without aggregating raw observations. However, frequent exchange of model updates can become the main bottleneck of communication. Therefore, one-shot approaches where each worker fits a local model and sends it to the server to aggregate emerge. It is known that averaging can achieve the so-called pooled-data mean squared error (MSE) order of a hypothetical node that has access to data from the server and all the workers, and performs empirical risk minimization (ERM) on it. However, when the number of workers increases too fast compared to the local sample size, nonzero local estimation bias prevents averaging from achieving this order.   In this paper, we study whether independent server data can overcome this limitation. We consider $m$ workers with $n$ observations each and a server with $p$ observations, all i.i.d., giving $N=mn+p$ observations in total. Under certain regularity conditions, a pooled-data ERM achieves MSE of order $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$. We analyze deterministic nonnegative averaging of convex-loss M-estimators, with equal worker weights and the server's own estimator included. Under our assumptions, including nonzero local bias of order $n^{-\alpha}$, $\alpha\geq1$, sample-size weighted averaging achieves the pooled-data MSE order whenever $m=\mathcal O(n^{2\alpha-1})$. Above this worker scale, it does so if and only if $p=\Omega(nm\cdot m/n^{2\alpha-1})$. Hence, server-only estimation, whose MSE is of order $\mathcal{O}(p^{-1})$, can achieve pooled-data order while sample-size weighting fails. Analytical examples and synthetic experiments illustrate when averaging matches the pooled-data MSE order, complemented by CIFAR-10 experiments comparing aggregation strategies with linear and nonlinear classifiers.
items.author: Pavle Tepav\v{c}evi\'{c}, Du\v{s}an Jakoveti\'{c}, Milo\v{s} Savi\'{c}
items.summary: Studies one-shot distributed learning where workers fit local models that the server aggregates, and proposes weighted averaging schemes incorporating server-side data to preserve the pooled-data MSE order even when the number of workers grows quickly relative to local sample sizes and local estimation bias is nonzero. This reduces communication relative to iterative distributed training.
items.reasoning: Communication-efficient distributed learning with theoretical guarantees (matching pooled-data MSE rates) is valuable for federated and cross-silo settings. The contribution is a refinement of known one-shot averaging results rather than a new paradigm, but the theory is useful.
